new_statements.rule_in_words: The source states no rule: it only says tone was left unmarked and primary/secondary stress are marked in the transcriptions. The penultimate reading is my provisional inference from the marked 100-item wordlist (pp. 16-25), where primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable in the large majority of di- and polysyllabic forms (léma, matháta, khothósa, letshoróma, sikínya, otséla..), with secondary stress on an earlier syllable in longer words (rurìfátsa, sekhwàripána, thùkhútha, bòdèdéma). Not a catalog-grade statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked with a grave accent on a syllable before the primary in longer words, typically two syllables before the primary (rurìfátsa, sìkínya, sekhwàripána, thùkhútha, kòmêlélo); no rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated by the authors; but the wordlist shows final primary stress in several nouns (mpšá 'dog', bòkokú 'grandmother', bofefú 'quickness', lekokú 'fever', swèlí 'cruelty', náaní, leínaní) and stress on an initial syllabic nasal in ńtsu 'eagle'; rough ALTO count pp. 16-25: 55 penult, 11 final, 8 antepenult (some scanned noise).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms elicited via a 100-item wordlist from 9 informants (I1-I9) in Tswapong villages (1992-94 survey); verbs cited with the infinitive marker (ho/xo) unstressed; stress marks appear on the abstract (orthographic) forms, not on the phonetic forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2006 ZDMG article describes Setswapong as spoken in the Tswapong Hills villages east of Palapye, Central District, Botswana (nine informants, 1992-94 survey; the authors note that some class it as a Sepedi/Northern Sotho rather than a Setswana dialect). This is the Botswana variety under tswa1237; the South African side is not covered.
